headline: Dysphoria botnet infects 200,000 devices, uses blockchain DNS & turns them into relays
summary: The Dysphoria botnet leverages blockchain name resolution and weak credentials to infect Linux devices, turning them into DDoS bots or relay nodes and exposing up to 155 ports. Daily infections peaked at 239,000 devices.
details: Dysphoria is a large-scale Linux botnet that infiltrates devices via weak Telnet/SSH passwords and various IoT RCE vulnerabilities. It obtains multi-stage C2 servers from ENS/SNS records, utilizing blockchain name resolution for command and control.

Infected devices are repurposed as DDoS bots or anonymous relay nodes, potentially exposing up to 155 ports on the local gateway using UPnP. Between July 14 and 20, 2026, daily infections reached a peak of 239,000 globally, with operators claiming control of about 200,000 devices.

The botnet's operators advertised up to 4 Tbps of DDoS capacity, though this figure is self-reported. The full architecture, persistence mechanisms, DDoS attack types, and regional infection counts have been detailed by researchers.

Devices in branch offices, factories, retail stores, security cameras, and remote work setups are vulnerable. When devices act as relay nodes, the assumption that "low traffic means safety" is no longer valid, necessitating monitoring of UPnP and outbound internal IoT traffic.

headline_marked: [[Opus 5 achieves 24% pass rate]] on SlopCodeBench, a new long-horizon coding benchmark
headline: Opus 5 achieves 24% pass rate on SlopCodeBench, a new long-horizon coding benchmark
summary: Anthropic's latest model, Opus 5, shows a modest improvement over previous models on the challenging multi-checkpoint benchmark, highlighting current LLM limitations in complex software engineering tasks.
details: A new long-horizon coding benchmark, SlopCodeBench, challenges LLMs by revealing problem requirements in multiple checkpoints, forcing models to evolve codebases over time. This contrasts with traditional benchmarks that disclose the entire problem upfront.
Previous top models, GPT-5.4 and Opus 4.6, achieved strict pass rates of 11% and 17% respectively on SlopCodeBench, indicating the benchmark is currently unsaturated.
Recent tests on a subset of SlopCodeBench involved Opus 5, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 5. Opus 5 technically won with a 24% strict pass rate, a slight increase over Opus 4.6's original 17%.

Despite the win, none of the models performed exceptionally well. Opus 5, for instance, showed a significant increase in verbosity and code complexity, writing five times more functions than Opus 4.8 for the same challenges.

The strict pass criteria meant that defects accumulated in earlier checkpoints prevented models from passing subsequent ones. None of the tested models made it to the end of any challenge without defects, even on an "easy" problem.

This performance suggests that current LLMs, even the most advanced, cannot be fully relied upon for real-world software engineering work that involves building solutions iteratively without constant human steering.

Opus 5 secured four strict passes (24% pass rate), while Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 each managed only one strict pass (6% pass rate). The results indicate that while more advanced models may offer slightly better correctness, no model achieved sufficient reliability.

The testing methodology involved running models in parallel with a fresh context window per checkpoint, using identical prompts within the Claude code harness. Defects were detected via black-box tests against the produced entrypoints.
